messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Caleb Whitmore is a 32-year-old single white American man who has worked as a park ranger in a remote national forest in the Pacific Northwest for the past six years. He presented for psychological assessment reporting a PCL-5 score of 41, approximately fourteen months after an incident in which he was abducted and tortured by a group of individuals he encountered while conducting a routine patrol of a backcountry trail. The details of what happened over those hours remain fragmented even in his own telling — when he attempts to describe the event in session, he loses the thread of the narrative mid-sentence, falling silent and shaking his head as though the words have simply dissolved. Some moments are seared into him with almost unbearable clarity: the particular quality of the light through a stand of Douglas fir, the sound of a door being pulled shut and locked from the outside, the sensation of his wrists against restraints. Others are entirely blank — stretches of time he cannot account for, which disturb him perhaps more than the memories he does carry. He cannot, he says, really put any of it into words. It is less a story he can tell than something that lives in his body.

In the weeks following his rescue and medical discharge, Caleb returned to his apartment and largely did not leave it. His injuries had been assessed as serious but non-life-threatening, yet he had come to believe something more permanent had been done to him — that his body was fundamentally compromised in ways the doctors had either missed or not told him. He monitors physical sensations with vigilance, interpreting aches or fatigue as confirmation of lasting damage. When his hands trembled during a routine task, he was certain it was evidence of something neurological. What frightened him almost as much as this conviction was the speed of his own reactions: before he could form a conscious thought, his body would already be responding — heart slamming, muscles bracing — to a sound outside or a shadow crossing the window. He had begun to fear that this gap between stimulus and awareness meant something was fundamentally broken in his mind, that the reactions he could not control were signs he was losing his grip on sanity.

Caleb stopped driving entirely in the months after the event. He had been transported in a vehicle during the abduction, and the enclosed space of a car — the inability to exit, the sense of being moved without control — had become intolerable. This has had direct consequences for his work. Park rangers in his district are required to conduct vehicle patrols across large areas of terrain, and his inability to drive or ride as a passenger has meant he has been placed on indefinite administrative reassignment, a situation that has deepened his isolation from colleagues and from the landscape that once gave his life structure and meaning. Before any interaction with his supervisor or the HR office, he rehearses the conversation at length — running through possible exchanges, preparing responses — because he had come to believe that other people could not be relied upon to behave predictably or safely, and that preparation was the only protection available to him. He checks the locks on his doors and windows multiple times each evening, and when a delivery is late or a message goes unanswered longer than he expects, he assumes something bad is unfolding — that the delay is not ordinary but ominous. He has described numbing his feelings as something he does deliberately, as a kind of management, though he acknowledges that what he is left with most of the time is a flat, exhausted distance from everything.

What finally brought Caleb to seek help was a conversation with his younger sister, who had driven four hours to visit him and found the apartment darkened, the locks checked, and her brother unable to explain to her what had happened or why he was living this way. He agreed to an intake appointment, though he came with considerable ambivalence. He is most afraid, he said quietly at the end of the first session, that the person he was before is simply gone. What he is hoping for, with something that looked like careful restraint, is to be told that is not true.
